content: Neonatal abstinence syndrome (NAS), which occurs due to opioid withdrawal in newborns, can lead to significant complications such as disruption of the mother-infant bond, sleep-wake disturbances, feeding difficulties, weight loss, seizures, and long-term neurodevelopmental issues. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of using opioids to treat NAS in newborns experiencing withdrawal from maternal opioid use during pregnancy. A total of 16 trials involving 1,110 infants were included in this analysis. These trials compared various opioid treatments to other interventions or supportive care. The findings are summarized below: 1. Opioid (Morphine) vs. No Treatment/Supportive Care Alone: A single trial involving 80 infants compared morphine plus supportive care to supportive care alone. There was no significant difference in treatment failure rates (risk ratio [RR] 1.29, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.41 to 4.07; very low certainty evidence). No seizures were reported in either group. Mortality, neurodevelopmental disability, and adverse events were not reported. Morphine use was associated with an increase in hospital stay duration (mean difference [MD] 15.00 days, 95% CI 8.86 to 21.14; very low certainty evidence) and treatment duration (MD 12.50 days, 95% CI 7.52 to 17.48; very low certainty evidence). However, morphine reduced the time to regain birthweight (MD -2.80 days, 95% CI -5.33 to -0.27) and the daily duration of supportive care required (MD -197.20 minutes, 95% CI -274.15 to -120.25). 2. Morphine vs. Methadone: Two studies involving 147 infants found no significant difference in treatment failure rates (RR 1.59, 95% CI 0.95 to 2.67; low certainty evidence). Seizures, mortality, and neurodevelopmental outcomes were not reported. One study reported no difference in hospital stay duration (MD 1.40 days, 95% CI -3.08 to 5.88; low certainty evidence), but two studies found an increase in treatment duration for morphine (MD 2.71 days, 95% CI 0.22 to 5.21; low certainty evidence). No differences were observed in breastfeeding rates, adverse events, or out-of-home placements. 3. Morphine vs. Sublingual Buprenorphine: Three studies involving 113 infants found no significant difference in treatment failure rates (RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.36 to 1.74; very low certainty evidence). Mortality and neurodevelopmental outcomes were not reported. Moderate certainty evidence indicated that morphine increased hospital stay duration (MD 11.45 days, 95% CI 5.89 to 17.01) and treatment duration (MD 12.79 days, 95% CI 7.57 to 18.00). A single adverse event (seizure) was reported in the buprenorphine group. 4. Morphine vs. Diluted Tincture of Opium (DTO): A single study involving 33 infants found no significant differences in hospital stay duration, treatment duration, or weight gain (low certainty evidence). 5. Opioid vs. Clonidine: A single study involving 31 infants reported no treatment failures in either group. Seizures, mortality, and neurodevelopmental outcomes were not reported. There was low certainty evidence for no difference in hospital stay or treatment duration. Adverse events were not reported. 6. Opioid vs. Diazepam: Two studies involving 86 infants showed a reduction in treatment failure with opioid use (RR 0.43, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.80; low certainty evidence). Seizures, mortality, and neurodevelopmental outcomes were not reported. A single study of 34 infants comparing methadone to diazepam found no difference in hospital stay or treatment duration (very low certainty evidence). Adverse events were not reported. 7. Opioid vs. Phenobarbital: Six studies involving 458 infants showed a reduction in treatment failure with opioid use (RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.74; moderate certainty evidence). Subgroup analysis revealed that trials using morphine at doses ≥0.5 mg/kg/day showed a significant reduction in treatment failure (RR 0.21, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.45; 3 studies, 230 infants), while a single study using lower doses (<0.5 mg/kg/day) found no difference compared to phenobarbital (subgroup difference P = 0.05). Mortality and neurodevelopmental outcomes were not reported. A single study of paregoric vs. phenobarbital reported seven seizures in the phenobarbital group, while no seizures were reported in two studies comparing morphine to phenobarbital. No differences were observed in hospital stay or treatment duration. A single study reported no adverse events in either group. 8. Opioid vs. Chlorpromazine: A single study involving 90 infants found a reduction in treatment failure with morphine compared to chlorpromazine (RR 0.08, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.62; moderate certainty evidence). No seizures were reported in either group. There was low certainty evidence for no difference in treatment duration. No adverse events were reported. None of the included studies provided data on the time required to control NAS. Additionally, data on the duration and severity of NAS were limited and could not be synthesized quantitatively. Conclusions: Adding an opioid to supportive care may increase the duration of hospital stay and treatment but may reduce the time to regain birthweight and the daily duration of supportive care. Opioids may reduce treatment failure compared to phenobarbital, diazepam, or chlorpromazine. The type of opioid used (e.g., morphine, methadone, buprenorphine) may have little to no effect on treatment failure rates. Buprenorphine likely reduces hospital stay and treatment duration compared to morphine, but there is insufficient evidence regarding its safety and time to control NAS. There is insufficient evidence to determine the effectiveness and safety of clonidine.
